common_name: Seleriana Air Plant (Bulbous Air Plant, Selerian Tillandsia)

planting.note: Mount on bark, driftwood, or wire in bright, filtered shade in zone 10-11, or grow as a houseplant elsewhere; unprotected plants are damaged below the low 40s°F. No soil or pot is needed since it is grown as a true epiphyte.

directions: Mount bare-root on bark, driftwood, or a wire hanger in bright, filtered shade and water by misting or soaking two to three times per week, letting the plant dry fully between waterings. Tillandsia seleriana is native to dry forests of Mexico and Central America and forms a distinctive swollen, bulbous base of silvery, heavily trichome-covered leaves that flare outward into a narrow, upright funnel shape, giving the whole plant an onion-like silhouette. The bulbous base offers some ant-nest habitat and moisture storage, which lets the plant tolerate drier, brighter conditions than many soft-leaved Tillandsia species, though outdoor Gulf South growers still find it thrives best tucked under high tree canopy rather than in open sun. A tall, branched, red-bracted flower spike with violet flowers rises above the foliage at maturity, after which offset pups form at the base and can be left in place to form a clustering colony.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil, siting well back from paths because of the vicious marginal spines; reliably hardy outdoors year-round only in zone 9b-11.

directions: Grow in partial shade to filtered sun beneath open tree canopy in well-drained soil, keeping the vigorously spreading clump away from walkways since every leaf edge is armed with hooked, curved spines. Bromelia pinguin is a large, terrestrial, thicket-forming bromeliad native from Mexico and the Caribbean through Central America into northern South America, long used in dooryard gardens and hedgerows as an impassable living fence around homesteads and pastures. The narrow, arching, silvery-green leaves flush pink to red toward the base as a tall central flower spike emerges, bearing small purple-and-pink flowers followed by yellow, edible, tart fruit that is traditionally used in beverages and preserves throughout its native range. Once established, the clump is extremely drought tolerant and spreads steadily by rhizomatous offsets, tolerating light, brief frost damage to the foliage tips while the root system persists through cool Gulf South winters in the warmest zones.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9-11; cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Use a well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix or orchid bark and keep the central cup filled with water.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light or deep filtered shade, as this florist hybrid tolerates lower light than nearly any other flowering houseplant bromeliad on the market. 'Orangeade' is a compact Guzmania cultivar selected for a dense, long-lasting inflorescence of solid, vivid orange bracts held well above a rosette of smooth, glossy, mid-green strap leaves, making it a popular grocery-store and garden-center gift plant. Keep the central leaf cup filled with fresh water and flush it every few weeks to prevent stagnation, and mist the foliage occasionally to mimic the humid understory conditions it would experience in habitat. Like all Guzmania, the parent rosette blooms only once and then slowly declines, but it produces offset pups at the base that can be separated once several inches tall and grown on into new flowering-size plants.

planting.note: Plant offsets in a well-drained, chunky mix in partial shade in zone 10-11, or grow in a large container elsewhere; damaged by temperatures below the mid-30s°F.

directions: Grow in partial shade under high canopy in a well-drained, chunky bark-based mix, giving this large bromeliad ample room since a mature rosette can span three feet or more across. Portea petropolitana is native to the coastal forests near Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where it grows both terrestrially and as an epiphyte on tree trunks, forming a broad rosette of stiff, silvery-gray, finely serrated leaves. In warm weather a tall, widely branched flower spike rises well above the foliage, carrying dozens of small lavender-purple flowers set off by pink bracts, followed by ornamental blue-purple berries that persist for weeks. Keep the central cup filled with water and flush it periodically; after the parent rosette flowers it gradually declines while producing offsets at the base that can be separated once well rooted.
